title: Chapter 112 — The Blacksmith
paragraphs: Taking advantage of the mild, summer-cool weather that now reigned in these latitudes, and in preparation for the especially active pursuits expected shortly, Perth, the begrimed, blistered old blacksmith, had not moved his portable forge back to the hold after finishing his share of the work on Ahab's leg, but kept it on deck, lashed fast to ringbolts by the foremast; for he was now almost constantly called on by the headsmen, and harpooners, and bowsmen to do some little job for them — altering, or repairing, or reshaping their various weapons and boat gear. Often he would be surrounded by an eager circle, all waiting to be served, holding boat-spades, pike-heads, harpoons and lances, and jealously watching his every sooty movement as he toiled. Nevertheless, this old man's was a patient hammer wielded by a patient arm. No murmur, no impatience, no petulance came from him. Silent, slow and solemn, bowing his chronically broken back still further, he toiled away as if toil were life itself, and the heavy beating of his hammer the heavy beating of his heart. And so it was. — Most miserable!

The old man walked in an odd way, with a slight lurch in his step that looked painful, and early in the voyage this had made the sailors curious. They had kept pestering him with questions until he finally gave in, and so now everyone knew the shameful story of his miserable fate.

Out late, and not innocently, one bitter winter midnight on the road between two country towns, the blacksmith, half-stupefied, felt the deadly numbness stealing over him, and took refuge in a leaning, dilapidated barn. The outcome was the loss of the ends of both his feet. From this revelation, piece by piece, there at last emerged the four acts of gladness, and the one long fifth act of grief, its catastrophe not yet reached, of his life's drama.

He was an old man who, at the age of nearly sixty, had belatedly encountered that thing called, in the technical language of sorrow, ruin. He had been a craftsman of famed excellence, with plenty to do; he owned a house and garden, embraced a youthful, daughter-like, loving wife and three merry, rosy-cheeked children, and every Sunday went to a cheerful-looking church planted in a grove. But one night, under cover of darkness, and further concealed in a most cunning disguise, a desperate burglar slid into his happy home and robbed them all of everything. And darker still to tell, it was the blacksmith himself who unknowingly led this burglar into the heart of his family. It was the Bottle Conjuror! When that fatal cork was drawn, out flew the fiend and shriveled up his home. Now, for prudent, most wise and economical reasons, the blacksmith's shop was in the basement of his house, but with a separate entrance of its own; so the young, loving, healthy wife had always listened — with no unhappy nervousness, but with vigorous pleasure — to the stout ringing of her young-armed old husband's hammer, whose echoes, muffled by passing through the floors and walls, came up to her, not unsweetly, in her nursery; and so, to stout Labor's iron lullaby, the blacksmith's infants were rocked to sleep.

Oh, woe on woe! Oh, Death, why can you not sometimes come in time? Had you taken this old blacksmith to yourself before his full ruin came upon him, then the young widow would have had a delicious grief, and her orphans a truly venerable, legendary father to dream of in their later years; and all of them a care-killing sufficiency to live on. But Death plucked down some virtuous elder brother, on whose whistling daily toil alone hung the responsibilities of some other family, and left the worse-than-useless old man standing, until the hideous rot of life should make him easier to harvest.

Why tell all of it? Every day the blows of the hammer in the basement came farther apart, and every day each blow was fainter than the one before. The wife sat frozen at the window, her eyes tearless and glittering as she stared into the weeping faces of her children. The bellows fell still; the forge clogged with cinders; the house was sold; the mother sank down into the long grass of the churchyard; twice her children followed her there; and the old man, without house or family, staggered off as a tramp in mourning crape, with no one to respect his sorrows, his gray head mocked by flaxen curls!

Death seems the only desirable sequel for a career like this; but Death is only a launching into the region of the strange Untried; it is only the first greeting to the possibilities of the immense Remote, the Wild, the Watery, the Unshored. Therefore, to the death-longing eyes of such men, who still have left in them some inward scruples against suicide, the all-contributed and all-receptive ocean alluringly spreads out his whole plain of unimaginable, captivating terrors and wonderful, new-life adventures; and from the hearts of infinite Pacifics the thousand mermaids sing to them: "Come to us, broken-hearted; here is another life without the guilt of dying in between; here are supernatural wonders, without dying for them. Come to us! Bury yourself in a life which, to your landed world, now equally abhorred and abhorring, is more oblivious than death. Come to us! You too, put up your gravestone within the churchyard, and come to us, till we marry you!"
Listening to these voices, East and West, at early sunrise and at nightfall, the blacksmith's soul answered: Aye, I come! And so Perth went a-whaling.
